original_value: Text-based games are a natural challenge domain for deep reinforcement learning algorithms. Their state and action spaces are combinatorially large, their reward function is sparse, and they are partially observable: the agent is informed of the consequences of its actions through textual feedback. In this paper we emphasize this latter point and consider the design of a deep reinforcement learning agent that can play from feedback alone. Our design recognizes and takes advantage of the structural characteristics of text-based games. We first propose a contextualisation mechanism, based on accumulated reward, which simplifies the learning problem and mitigates partial observability. We then study different methods that rely on the notion that most actions are ineffectual in any given situation, following Zahavy et al.'s idea of an admissible action. We evaluate these techniques in a series of text-based games of increasing difficulty based on the TextWorld framework, as well as the iconic game Zork. Empirically, we find that these techniques improve the performance of a baseline deep reinforcement learning agent applied to text-based games.

result.paraphrase: Text-based games present a natural challenge for deep reinforcement learning because their state and action spaces are combinatorially large, rewards are sparse, and they are partially observable: the agent learns the effects of its actions through textual feedback. In this paper, we focus on that last aspect and study the design of a deep reinforcement learning agent that can play using feedback alone. Our approach exploits the structural properties of text-based games. We first introduce a contextualization mechanism based on accumulated reward, which eases learning and reduces partial observability. We then examine several methods built on the idea that, in a given situation, most actions are ineffective, following Zahavy et al.'s notion of an admissible action. We test these techniques on a set of text-based games of increasing difficulty from the TextWorld framework, along with the classic game Zork. Experiments show that these methods improve the performance of a baseline deep reinforcement learning agent in text-based games.
